title: Big Boy Pants
subtitle: Being a parent mens having hard conversations, once you have built trust.
body_html:
My son is eight years old. My daughter is also eight years old. The defining moments as a parent are not necessarily the ones you would choose. Kids learn from what we say. They learn more, however, from what we do. They learn when we're kind. They learn when we're angry. They learn when we're vindictive. Kids are noticing champions. Interpreting—as their parents would like—isn’t their core competency.

Children are constantly learning because they have so much to learn. It's a complicated world; they need values and knowledge to get through it. We're not communicating those values and facts to little humans absent any temperament or inclinations. Our children are made of the same stuff that made their parents. You can have a plan for where you're going to teach your kids all day long, but what they're going to learn might be different.

What is the difference between internalized lessons that become part of your kid's moral fiber and those that are interesting…but irrelevant? Often, the amount of trust you've built determines that difference. Trust in social information is the bedrock—Dr. Peter Fonagy from the Anna Freud Centre called this “epistemic trust.” I’ll let him explain:

Some lessons are incorporated incredibly rapidly. “No, don’t take candy from the man in the free candy van” is a relatively complex lesson. They must hear the words and understand what they mean. They also must trust that you have their best interest in your heart. Without that trust, kids are going to assume that you're just trying to keep them away from great candy.

Share

If they watch you, and they will watch you, and you also refrain from the free candy? Suddenly, credibility goes up 1000-fold. Imagine they've never seen you take free candy from a bad man. Now, suddenly, you have the track record and trustworthy demeanor of somebody who can say, “Let's pass on that free candy…” and is believable.

My daughter doesn't like McDonald's. I took her trick-or-treating, and she didn't take most of the candy. She didn't want it. It was sweet and too unhealthy, and she planned to share half of what she did bring home with her mommy. I never told her to do that, but she did learn those things for herself, from how we acted.

Not every lesson is explicit. The most important lessons are communicated without words. They are communicated by first building a record of trustworthy behavior so your words are interesting and relevant. If your kids feel understood, everything you say has a better chance of overcoming the barrier of mistrust.

Mistrust is adaptive. You shouldn't just trust everybody. Some people do not have your best interest at heart. Some individuals are predatory, and some are Buzzkill, and avoiding both is what kids should do. When school is boring, they're not wrong that school is boring. It's normal to avoid things that are boring. We're not supposed to trust liars; you wouldn't want your kids getting scammed.

And yet, many of us get scammed, and many of our kids could also be susceptible. Crooks? They understand the role of trust. With everything they do, they telegraph that they should be trusted—blindly. And this, too, can be a bucket of lies—scammers must be liars to do their job. Every lesson we teach our kids is about the trust we want to build with them and the mistrust we want them to have in the context that it protects them.

My kids were disappointed after the election. My son wanted to understand how people could believe things so contrary to his beliefs. My daughter wanted a girl president. “Why can’t we have that?” she wailed. Democracy is an exercise in frustration for parents. Our responses teach our kids what to expect from others and how to respond to their feelings. We're teaching trust and mistrust at the same time, inadvertently. We teach through our actions and kindness. Every moment is teachable.

Teaching children to talk about their thoughts and feelings when upset isn’t really “teaching” in the traditional sense—we are all born with this capacity.

However, when the stakes are high, the safest assumption about the minds of others is that you can’t know for sure what is inside them.

I’ve written a book on this topic (Mentalizing) (amazon affiliate link). Peter Fonagy has written several, including this fundamental text.
